title: Team relationship to technology
question: What technology does this team actually own or steward?

items.description: Teams dissolve after projects. Technology ownership is incidental.
Teams grouped by expertise in particular technologies. They do not own running systems. Ownership sits elsewhere.
Teams organized around administering and integrating specific external systems.
Teams own parts of the architecture or infrastructure stack.
Teams own a reusable capability in the value chain. They provide services to multiple products or domains.
Teams own a combination of technologies primarily in service of a business domain, problem domain, or value stream.

title: Team relationship to customers
question: Who interacts with customers, and how does customer understanding reach the team?

items.description: Customers submit requests. Teams fulfill them. Little or no shared understanding of underlying needs.
Intermediary roles (sales, account managers, analysts, business stakeholders) interact with customers and interpret needs for the team.
Product managers or designers interact directly with customers. They synthesize insights and shape team understanding.
Some team members interact directly with customers and participate in discovery and shared understanding.
The entire team regularly interacts with customers. Customer insight and synthesis are shared team responsibilities.

title: Team relationship to funding
question: Why does this team receive budget and headcount?

items.description: Teams funded to deliver a specific project. Funding ends when the project ends.
Teams funded using staffing ratios tied to requests, tickets, users, or managed tools.

items.principle: Program or project-attached funding with BAU remnant
items.description: Teams funded through participation in funded programs and/or projects, plus residual operational ownership.
Teams funded as an allocation against a product, business line, or revenue stream.
Teams funded through internal chargeback or showback. Funding scales with actual service consumption.
Teams funded through annual budget or capacity planning based on forecasted demand, rather than per-work approval.

Teams funded based on explicit claims about revenue growth, revenue protection, or cost reduction, typically argued through proxy metrics or intermediate concepts that teams can influence more directly.
Teams funded based on their role in increasing system throughput, reducing bottlenecks, or improving flow efficiency, rather than direct project delivery or revenue attribution.
Teams funded according to the investment logic of the product’s lifecycle stage (New Offerings, Strategic Expansion, Growth Accelerator, Margin Optimization, Operational Optimizer, Reset & Repair).

title: How team performance is assessed
question: What does this team get praised or criticized for?

items.description: Teams assessed on on-time and predictable delivery of predefined work.
Teams assessed on volume of delivered features, requests, or completed work items.
Teams assessed on delivering usable product that stakeholders or customers accept as meeting stated needs.
Teams assessed on demonstrated improvement in customer experience or behavior, indicating that real customer problems have been solved.

Teams assessed on their ability to influence actionable inputs or leading indicators that are explicitly modeled in causal chains linked to customer outcomes, business outcomes, or North Star Metrics.
Teams assessed using financial proxy metrics such as margin contribution, cost per transaction, or revenue per user.
Teams assessed on cycle time, throughput, work-in-progress, queue health, or reliability of flow through the system.
Teams assessed on direct signals of customer experience such as satisfaction ratings, NPS, support volume, sentiment, or qualitative feedback.
Teams assessed on reliability, operational stability, security posture, or risk reduction, often expressed through incident rates, uptime, or compliance metrics.
Teams assessed on how effectively they enable or amplify the productivity of other teams through platforms, tooling, or shared services.
Teams assessed on rate of discovery, experimentation, or validated learning in uncertain problem spaces.

title: Team relationship to work
question: Where does this team's work actually come from?

items.description: Work originates from externally submitted requests. Requests are triaged, prioritized, and sometimes lightly researched before entering the team.
Work originates from requirements specified by business analysts, systems analysts, or similar intermediary roles, and then decomposed into team work items.
Work originates from research into user or stakeholder goals and unmet needs, leading to newly defined work.
Work originates from identified opportunities. Teams explore and propose solution paths before committing to delivery work.
Work originates as experiments designed to test hypotheses or achieve defined outcomes or goals.
Work originates from production issues, telemetry, reliability needs, or system health signals.
Work originates from direct managerial direction or task assignment.
Work originates from internally proposed ideas that gain traction through influence, advocacy, or leadership preference rather than formal discovery or demand signals.
Work originates from the most immediate crisis, escalation, or urgent operational need at the time. Priority is set by perceived urgency rather than planned intent.

title: How high level intent is communicated
question: How is strategy or direction communicated to this team?

items.description: High-level intent is expressed as approved projects or programs. Teams receive defined initiatives rather than abstract context.
High-level intent is expressed as broad priority areas. Teams interpret these into concrete work.
High-level intent is expressed as specific problems to solve. Teams determine solutions.
High-level intent is expressed as opportunity spaces to explore. Teams investigate and shape possible directions.
High-level intent is expressed as desired outcomes or goals. Teams define local objectives or initiatives to achieve them.
High-level intent is expressed primarily through financial targets, forecasts, or line-item plans. Strategy discussions center on revenue, cost, or margin expectations.
High-level intent is expressed through mission, customer promise, or strategic narrative without explicit financial targets.
High-level intent communicates explicit choices about what will and will not be pursued. Teams operate within defined strategic boundaries.
High-level intent provides direction but leaves trade-offs and choices largely to teams or local leadership.

title: Team mandate levels
question: What kind of mandate is this team being given?

items.description: Teams are asked to build exactly what is specified to a predetermined definition.
Teams are asked to build something that performs specific behaviors, interactions, or input–output functions.
Teams are asked to build something that allows a segment of users or customers to complete a defined task or goal.
Teams are asked to solve an open-ended customer problem, with freedom in solution approach.
Teams are asked to explore challenges and improve the experience for a segment of users or customers.
Teams are asked to increase or decrease a specific metric known to influence a business outcome.
Teams are asked to explore potential intervention points and run experiments to influence a business outcome.
Teams are asked to directly produce a near-term business result.
Teams are asked to build enduring capabilities or systems that produce sustained long-term business outcomes.
